text:
Training many different machine learning models and averaging their predictions is a very simple way to improve performance [P3_p1_c02]. However, making predictions using a whole ensemble of models is cumbersome and may be too computationally expensive to allow deployment to a large number of users, especially if the individual models are large neural networks [P3_p1_c02]. 

This paper shows that it is possible to compress the knowledge in an ensemble into a single model that is much easier to deploy [P3_p1_c02]. The paper develops this approach further using a different compression technique called distillation [P3_p1_c02][P3_p2_c04]. 

When models discriminate between a large number of classes, they assign probabilities to all incorrect answers [P3_p2_c01]. The relative probabilities of these incorrect answers tell us a lot about how the model generalizes [P3_p2_c01]. For example, a BMW may have a very small chance of being mistaken for a garbage truck, but that mistake is much more probable than mistaking it for a carrot [P3_p2_c01]. 

The paper achieves surprising results on MNIST and significantly improves the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system by distilling knowledge into a single model [P3_p1_c02]. The research also introduces a new type of ensemble composed of full models and specialist models [P3_p1_c02]. These specialist models learn to distinguish fine-grained classes that the full models confuse, and they can be trained rapidly and in parallel [P3_p1_c02].
